newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian protesters step up strikes, blockades.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian protesters step up strikes, blockades.

text.p: Bulgarian protesters stepped up strikes, rallies and blockades on Thursday, unmoved by an appeal from the ex-communist ruling Socialists for talks to set an election date.

At the town of Doupnitsa, south of Sofia, hundreds of protesters have blocked the main road and railway to Greece since Wednesday morning. Working in shifts, they kept up the blockade overnight, burning tyres to keep warm.
In Bulgaria's second city of Plovdiv, taxis and buses blocked main junctions in the city centre. Sofia city transport stopped work for an hour.
The Confederation of Independent Trade Unions said the strikes had more support than on Wednesday. "In almost every town and village there are one-hour strikes," a spokeswoman said.
Miners in Pernik held an early morning protest rally and a minute's silence for colleagues who died in accidents at work.

Bulgaria, its economy in ruins, has been plunged into its worst crisis since the fall of communism in 1989 by 25 days of demonstrations calling for quick elections and an end to rule by the Socialists, who won parliamentary elections in 1994.
Socialist Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, who is trying to form an interim government, warned on Wednesday that "the chaos and power vacuum may threaten civil peace".

The main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) was quick to reject Dobrev's offer to stand down at an agreed date in the next three to five months and hold elections, saying it wanted the vote now.
The Socialists have overseen a caretaker government since prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned in December after his party suffered a landslide loss in presidential elections.
They have an absolute majority in parliament but the UDF is trying to win enough Socialist defections to prevent Dobrev from forming a government.
The lev currency has plummeted, inflation has soared and the government has warned it may default on its $10 billion foreign debt.
The lev was quoted at 1,300-1,650 per dollar on the interbank market on Thursday. Technicians had to reset banks' software on Tuesday to accept four-figure quotes.
Troud daily carried a table showing the minimum monthly wage of 5,500 levs was worth $3.90, and the average wage of 20,000 levs $14.30, while an average pension of 5,665 levs was worth $4.

Referring to mass protests in Albania, once a byword for Balkan backwardness, it compared the figures with an average Albanian wage of 8,000 leks, worth $72, and an average Albanian pension of 3,000 leks, worth $27.
The main branch of the State Savings Bank was swamped on Wednesday with clients withdrawing funds and foreign exchange booths around Sofia were packed with people changing levs for dollars.
Long queues formed at petrol stations on fears that state oil refineries would run dry for lack of money.
Dobrev, in his interview on state television, appeared determined that the Socialists should form a new government and have a breathing space before taking the country to the polls.
He said a package of emergency measures must be agreed and passed by parliament immediately to save the Bulgarian economy from complete collapse.
The opposition street protests have often been colourful and imaginative. Students held a candle-light parade and a spoof Miss Protest and Mr Vagabond contest on Wednesday.
To a blaring rock version of the national anthem, women students paraded in military uniforms or lingerie under coats and boasted names such as Miss Kalashnikov or Miss Flakjacket.
One student dressed as a corpse carried a sign saying "Bulgarian".
